questions.stem: A public health team studies an X-linked recessive enzyme deficiency in an isolated population that is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Newborn screening results are: boys screened 40,000, boys affected 8; girls screened 40,000, girls affected 0. Every affected boy carries the same mutant allele. What is the approximate frequency of heterozygous carriers among women in this population?
choices: 1 in 35
questions.explanation: Males have one X, so the **frequency of affected boys equals q**: 8/40,000 = **1/5,000**. Carrier women = **2pq ≈ 2q = 2/5,000 = 1/2,500**. The tempting 1 in 5,000 is q itself, the allele frequency, not the carrier frequency. The value 1 in 35 comes from treating 1/5,000 as an autosomal recessive incidence: q = √(1/5,000) ≈ 1/71, and 2q ≈ 1/35; 1 in 25,000,000 (q²) is the expected rate of affected girls, which fits the zero affected girls found.
questions.explanation_pt: Os homens têm um único X, então a **frequência de meninos afetados é igual a q**: 8/40.000 = **1/5.000**. Mulheres portadoras = **2pq ≈ 2q = 2/5.000 = 1/2.500**. A resposta tentadora 1 em 5.000 é o próprio q, a frequência do alelo, e não a de portadoras. O valor 1 em 35 vem de tratar 1/5.000 como incidência de doença autossômica recessiva: q = √(1/5.000) ≈ 1/71 e 2q ≈ 1/35; já 1 em 25.000.000 (q²) é a taxa esperada de meninas afetadas, compatível com nenhuma menina afetada encontrada.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay. He spoke his first words at age 3, avoids eye contact, flaps his hands and is very hyperactive. He has a long, narrow face and large ears that stick out. His mother's menstrual periods stopped at age 34. His maternal grandfather, now 69, has developed a tremor when he uses his hands and an unsteady gait over the past 3 years. DNA testing in the boy shows more than 300 copies of a trinucleotide repeat in the 5' untranslated region of a gene on the X chromosome. Which mechanism best explains the boy's disease?
choices: Toxic gain of function of mRNA that carries the expanded repeat
Methylation of the gene's promoter, which silences transcription
A long polyglutamine tract that makes the protein clump in neurons
An intronic repeat that lowers transcription of a mitochondrial iron protein
Absence of active paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15
questions.explanation: This is **fragile X syndrome**: a **full mutation** (over 200 CGG repeats) in *FMR1* leads to **methylation of the promoter**, so the gene is not transcribed and **FMRP** is absent. Toxic mRNA gain of function is tempting, but it is the mechanism of the **premutation** (about 55-200 repeats), which explains the grandfather's late-onset tremor and ataxia and the mother's early ovarian failure. The premutation expanded to a full mutation when the mother passed it on. A polyglutamine tract describes CAG diseases such as Huntington disease.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se da **síndrome do X frágil**: uma **mutação completa** (mais de 200 repetições CGG) no *FMR1* leva à **metilação do promotor**, de modo que o gene não é transcrito e a **FMRP** está ausente. O ganho de função tóxico do mRNA é tentador, mas é o mecanismo da **pré-mutação** (cerca de 55-200 repetições), que explica o tremor e a ataxia de início tardio do avô e a insuficiência ovariana prematura da mãe. A pré-mutação expandiu-se para mutação completa quando a mãe a transmitiu. Um trato de poliglutamina descreve as doenças por CAG, como a doença de Huntington.

questions.stem: A man and a woman who have both been profoundly deaf since birth meet at a school for deaf students. They later have four children, and all four have normal hearing. In each spouse's family, the parents had normal hearing and were first cousins, and only that one sibship had deafness. Neither spouse has features of a syndrome or a history of congenital infection. Genetic testing confirms that each spouse has autosomal recessive nonsyndromic deafness. Which concept best explains why all of their children hear normally?
choices: Incomplete penetrance
Allelic heterogeneity
Germline mosaicism
Variable expressivity
Locus heterogeneity
questions.explanation: Mutations in **different genes** can cause the same phenotype (**locus heterogeneity**). Each spouse is homozygous at a different locus, so every child is a heterozygous carrier at both loci and has one working copy of each gene. Allelic heterogeneity is tempting, but it means different mutations in the **same** gene; then each child would inherit two mutant alleles of that gene and be deaf. Incomplete penetrance would not explain normal hearing in all four children.
questions.explanation_pt: Mutações em **genes diferentes** podem causar o mesmo fenótipo (**heterogeneidade de locus**). Cada cônjuge é homozigoto em um locus diferente, então cada filho é portador heterozigoto nos dois loci e tem uma cópia funcional de cada gene. A heterogeneidade alélica é tentadora, mas significa mutações diferentes no **mesmo** gene; nesse caso, cada filho herdaria dois alelos mutantes desse gene e seria surdo. A penetrância incompleta não explicaria a audição normal nos quatro filhos.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman's first pregnancy ended at 30 weeks with a stillborn baby who had short, bent limbs, many fractures of different ages, beaded ribs and a soft, poorly mineralized skull. Testing of the baby showed a heterozygous glycine substitution in COL1A1. Both parents are healthy, with white sclerae and no fractures, and the variant was not found in DNA from their blood. Two years later, ultrasound in her second pregnancy with the same partner again shows many fractures, and the same COL1A1 variant is found in the fetus. Which mechanism best explains the recurrence?
choices: Autosomal recessive inheritance from two carrier parents
Incomplete penetrance of the variant in one healthy parent
Presence of the variant in some germ cells of one parent
Uniparental disomy of the chromosome that carries COL1A1
Expansion of an unstable repeat in a parent's germline
questions.explanation: Lethal perinatal **osteogenesis imperfecta** usually comes from a new **dominant** *COL1A1* or *COL1A2* mutation. When the **same** new variant appears in two pregnancies but not in the parents' blood, a parent carries it in part of the germline (**germline mosaicism**). Autosomal recessive inheritance is tempting because healthy parents had two affected children, but the fetus has only one mutant allele, and the parents' blood is negative. Incomplete penetrance would require the variant in a parent's blood cells.
questions.explanation_pt: A **osteogênese imperfeita** perinatal letal geralmente resulta de uma mutação nova **dominante** em *COL1A1* ou *COL1A2*. Quando a **mesma** variante nova aparece em duas gestações, mas não no sangue dos pais, um dos genitores a carrega em parte da linhagem germinativa (**mosaicismo germinativo**). A herança autossômica recessiva é tentadora porque pais saudáveis tiveram dois filhos afetados, mas o feto tem apenas um alelo mutante e o sangue dos pais é negativo. A penetrância incompleta exigiria a variante nas células sanguíneas de um dos pais.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the clinic because she bled for 3 days after a wisdom tooth was removed, and her menstrual periods are heavy. Her father has hemophilia A. Her mother and her mother's relatives have no bleeding problems. Laboratory studies show: platelet count 260,000/mm³; PT 12 seconds (normal 11-13); aPTT 49 seconds (normal 25-35); factor VIII activity 12% (normal 50-150); von Willebrand factor antigen, activity and factor VIII binding normal. Her karyotype is 46,XX, and F8 gene testing shows one mutant allele and one normal allele. Which mechanism best explains her low factor VIII level?
choices: Skewed X inactivation in the cells that make factor VIII
Half the normal F8 gene dose, as expected in every carrier
Loss of one X chromosome from all of her cells
Uniparental disomy of her father's X chromosome
Fast clearance of factor VIII due to defective von Willebrand factor
questions.explanation: Each female cell randomly silences one X (**lyonization**). In this carrier, most factor VIII-producing cells by chance kept the X with the **mutant** *F8* active (**skewed X inactivation**), so her level is far below what one normal allele usually gives. A simple half dose is tempting, but random inactivation leaves most carriers near 50%, which is usually enough to prevent abnormal bleeding; 12% is much lower. A 46,XX karyotype rules out X loss, one normal allele rules out paternal uniparental disomy, and normal von Willebrand factor tests rule out a carrier-protein defect.
questions.explanation_pt: Cada célula feminina silencia aleatoriamente um X (**lionização**). Nesta portadora, por acaso, a maioria das células produtoras de fator VIII manteve ativo o X com o *F8* **mutante** (**inativação desviada, não aleatória, do X**), de modo que seu nível fica muito abaixo do que um alelo normal costuma garantir. Uma simples dose pela metade é tentadora, mas a inativação aleatória mantém a maioria das portadoras perto de 50%, o que geralmente basta para evitar sangramento anormal; 12% é muito menos. O cariótipo 46,XX exclui perda do X, o alelo normal exclui dissomia uniparental paterna, e os testes normais do fator de von Willebrand excluem defeito da proteína carreadora.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. He is tall and has small, firm testes, and semen analysis shows no sperm. His karyotype is 47,XXY. To find the origin of the extra X chromosome, the family is tested with a highly variable DNA marker that lies next to the X centromere, so crossing over rarely separates it from the centromere. Results (allele sizes): mother 182 and 190 base pairs; father 186 base pairs; patient 182 and 190 base pairs. The patient's Y-chromosome markers match his father's. In which cell division did the error most likely occur?
choices: Maternal meiosis II
Paternal meiosis I
Paternal meiosis II
Maternal meiosis I
Mitosis in the early embryo
questions.explanation: The patient has **both different maternal alleles** and no paternal X, so the two **homologous** maternal X chromosomes failed to separate: **maternal meiosis I nondisjunction**. Maternal meiosis II is the tempting answer, but failed separation of **sister chromatids** would give two copies of the same allele (182 and 182, or 190 and 190) at a marker near the centromere. A paternal meiosis I error would make an XY sperm, so the patient would carry the 186 allele, and paternal meiosis II cannot produce an XY sperm. An error in early embryonic mitosis would duplicate one X and also give identical alleles.
questions.explanation_pt: O paciente tem **os dois alelos maternos diferentes** e nenhum X paterno, então os dois cromossomos X maternos **homólogos** não se separaram: **não disjunção na meiose I materna**. A meiose II materna é a resposta tentadora, mas a falha na separação das **cromátides-irmãs** daria duas cópias do mesmo alelo (182 e 182, ou 190 e 190) em um marcador próximo ao centrômero. Um erro na meiose I paterna geraria um espermatozoide XY, e o paciente teria o alelo 186; a meiose II paterna não pode gerar espermatozoide XY. Um erro na mitose do embrião inicial duplicaria um X e também daria alelos idênticos.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man asks about the risk to his future children. Since early childhood he has had bowed legs, and he is short. He has had several tooth abscesses without cavities. His mother and his sister have the same condition. Laboratory studies show: calcium 9.4 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5); phosphate 1.9 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5); PTH normal; 25-hydroxyvitamin D normal; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D low-normal; urine phosphate excretion high; FGF23 high. Genetic testing shows a pathogenic variant in the *PHEX* gene on the X chromosome. His wife is healthy and has no family history of bone disease. Which outcome is expected in their children?
choices: Each child of either sex has a 50% risk
All daughters affected and no sons affected
All sons affected and no daughters affected
Daughters are healthy carriers and sons are healthy
Each son has a 50% risk and daughters are unaffected
questions.explanation: The *PHEX* variant confirms **X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets**, which is **X-linked dominant**. A father gives his only X to **every daughter**, and one mutant copy is enough to cause disease, so all daughters are affected; sons receive his Y and are unaffected. A 50% risk for each child is tempting, but it applies to an affected **mother** or to autosomal dominant disease. Daughters are not silent carriers, because in a dominant disorder one mutant allele causes the disease.
questions.explanation_pt: A variante em *PHEX* confirma **raquitismo hipofosfatêmico ligado ao X**, de herança **dominante ligada ao X**. O pai transmite seu único X a **todas as filhas**, e uma cópia mutante basta para causar a doença, então todas as filhas são afetadas; os **filhos homens** recebem o Y e não são afetados. Um risco de 50% para cada **criança, de qualquer sexo**, é tentador, mas vale para uma **mãe** afetada ou para doença autossômica dominante. As filhas não são portadoras silenciosas, porque em uma doença dominante um alelo mutante causa a doença.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for severe developmental delay. She does not speak, walks with a stiff, jerky, wide-based gait, has seizures and often laughs at unexpected times. Her head is small. DNA methylation at 15q11-q13 is normal, and FISH shows no deletion. Sequencing shows a loss-of-function mutation in UBE3A. Her healthy mother carries the same mutation, and family testing shows that the mother inherited it from her own healthy father. What is the best estimate of the chance that the couple's next child will have the same disorder?
choices: Less than 1%
questions.explanation: This is **Angelman syndrome**: in neurons only the **maternal** *UBE3A* allele is active, because the paternal allele is silenced by imprinting. The mother is healthy because her mutant copy came from her **father**, so it is the silent allele in her brain. Each child she has receives the mutant allele with a **50%** chance, and in the child it is now maternal and causes disease. Less than 1% is tempting because it fits a new deletion or uniparental disomy, but a point mutation carried by the mother gives a high recurrence risk.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se da **síndrome de Angelman**: nos neurônios, apenas o alelo **materno** do *UBE3A* é ativo, porque o alelo paterno é silenciado por imprinting. A mãe é saudável porque sua cópia mutante veio do **pai** dela, sendo, portanto, o alelo silencioso em seu cérebro. Cada filho dela recebe o alelo mutante com chance de **50%**, e na criança ele passa a ser materno e causa a doença. Menos de 1% é tentador porque vale para uma deleção nova ou dissomia uniparental, mas uma mutação pontual presente na mãe dá alto risco de recorrência.
